title: The Stopwatch and the Heartbeat: Brooklyn, Judson, and Fifty Years of Dancing Made Visible
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Brooklyn, born in the winter of 1944
stops.date_confidence: attested; birth date and borough confirmed by Wikipedia, 'Sara Rudner,' and by Rudner's own self-authored 2015 profile. No hospital is named in any reachable source.
stops.campa: A daughter is born in Brooklyn in the winter of the war's last full year, to parents whose own parents came out of Russia. She will put the borough first whenever she describes herself, ahead of any training and any company. No hospital is recorded, and no ceremony. What survives is the date. The sixteenth of February will still be the operative one thirty-two years later, when she marks her thirty-second birthday by making thirty-two separate dances in a loft on Broadway.
stops.quote: I was born in February 1944, and lived until the age of 17 in Brooklyn, New York...
stops.quote_source: Sara Rudner, self-authored profile, Life as a Modern Dancer, 'Dancing and Reflecting: Dancers in Their 70s' (2015)
suggested_refs: Rudner's self-authored profile at life-as-a-modern-dancer.com, the fullest first-person account of her Brooklyn childhood
sources: Wikipedia, 'Sara Rudner'
Sara Rudner, Life as a Modern Dancer profile (2015)

stops.name: East Twenty-seventh Street, a house at the end of the line
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the address 960 East 27th Street is a dossier lead attributed to a Barnard College 1964 yearbook that could not be retrieved. The date is a placeholder for early childhood, not an event.
stops.campa: The family lives out near Brooklyn College, at the end of the Flatbush line, where the subway stops being a subway. There is money for dance lessons or for music lessons, not for both, and the choice falls to dance. The street is residential and unremarkable. Nothing in it predicts a career, and nothing in the record says the family expected one. She measures the address in subway stops rather than in blocks. The ride into Manhattan is the first long journey she makes regularly.
suggested_refs: The Barnard College 1964 yearbook, sole carrier for the childhood address and for the name Sara Mae Rudner
sources: Dossier lead only; the underlying yearbook page was not reachable in this pass

stops.name: Avenue I, Bella Malinka's basement barre
stops.date_confidence: partly attested; Wikipedia confirms early ballet study with Bella Malinka at a neighborhood music school. The address at East 29th Street and Avenue I, and the age of nine, are reconstruction. Coordinates corrected 1.2 km north from the gathered figure, which fell near Avenue P.
stops.campa: In a music-school basement near Avenue I a teacher named Bella Malinka takes the nine-year-old through barre, then centre, then eventually pointe. The uniform is a black cotton leotard and bare legs, soft slippers at first and pointe shoes later. This is not a conservatory, and Malinka is not a famous name; it is a neighborhood arrangement, ballet delivered at the price a Brooklyn family can pay. A mother of one of the students sits at an upright and plays Chopin waltzes while the girls work.
stops.quote: Black cotton leotards, naked legs, soft slippers and then pointe shoes at the barre.
stops.quote_source: Sara Rudner, Life as a Modern Dancer profile (2015)
sources: Wikipedia, 'Sara Rudner'
Sara Rudner, Life as a Modern Dancer profile (2015)

stops.name: Midwood High School, out at sixteen
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the school, the 1956-1960 span, the accelerated examination track and the typing all rest on Rudner's own recollection as relayed in dossier material and are confirmed by no fetched source. Coordinates corrected to 2839 Bedford Avenue.
stops.campa: She enters Midwood High School rather than the High School of Performing Arts; the family declines the audition track, and dance stays an after-school matter. An accelerated examination program carries her through in four years and out at sixteen. She learns typing there. The skill looks incidental beside ballet and modern class, and it is not: clerical work is what pays her rent through the unpaid downtown years to come. All of this rests on her own recollection. No fetched source names the school.
sources: Dossier lead only, from Rudner's own account; not independently confirmed

stops.name: Barnard College, arriving with nothing to unlearn
stops.date_confidence: attested for the degree, which Wikipedia and Rudner's own bio in Christopher Janney's 2025 retrospective both carry. The years 1960-1964 and the Russian-studies major appear in neither and are reconstruction.
stops.campa: She crosses the river to Morningside Heights, commuting from Brooklyn the first year and then living near the campus. Here the first sustained modern-dance classes happen, alongside a degree the record confirms without describing. She has had no art training and says so plainly, calling herself almost a blank slate. She is not being modest. She means she arrived with no method to unlearn and nothing to defend, and she is still using the phrase about herself fifty years later, in an interview about the early Tharp years.
stops.quote: I was a New York City kid, born and raised in Brooklyn. I had no art training.
stops.quote_source: Wendy Perron, 'Sara Rudner on Early Tharp,' wendyperron.com (1 December 2015)
sources: Wikipedia, 'Sara Rudner'
Christopher Janney, '40 Years Passing By In (A) HeartBeat' (2025), Rudner bio
Wendy Perron, 'Sara Rudner on Early Tharp' (2015)

stops.name: New London, a summer at the American Dance Festival
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; dossier lead only. No program or festival record was located for the Pearl Lang revival or for Rudner's participation.
stops.campa: She spends a summer at the American Dance Festival on the Connecticut College campus, where American modern dance concentrates itself annually into one small New England town, and dances in a revival of Pearl Lang's And Joy Is My Witness. Lang's work descends directly from Graham, and learning a repertory piece from the generation above is a young dancer's ordinary way in. No program or festival record of that summer could be located; the residency survives only in her own chronology. She is twenty years old.
suggested_refs: American Dance Festival programs, Connecticut College, summer 1964
sources: Dossier lead only; unconfirmed

stops.name: West Twenty-first Street, the Sanasardo company
stops.date_confidence: sequence attested: Wikipedia states she performed with Paul Sanasardo before joining Tharp's company in 1965. The 1964 date, the studio address and the named roles are reconstruction, carried by the dossier alone.
stops.campa: She studies intensively with Paul Sanasardo and dances in his company, in a studio on West Twenty-first Street near Sixth Avenue. Sanasardo's work is dramatic and weighted, built on trained modern technique, and roles in Excursions, The Animal's Eye and Fatal Birds are credited to her. It is the last conventional apprenticeship she will serve. Within a year she is working for a choreographer who measures a room heel to toe with a stopwatch and calls the result a dance.
stops.quote: I was really almost a blank slate.
stops.quote_source: Wendy Perron, 'Sara Rudner on Early Tharp,' wendyperron.com (1 December 2015)
sources: Wikipedia, 'Sara Rudner'
Wendy Perron, 'Sara Rudner on Early Tharp' (2015)

stops.name: Judson Hall, She'll do
stops.date_confidence: tradition. The line is confirmed verbatim in Perron's 2015 interview, but as a single chain of testimony: Jenkins told Rudner, Rudner tells Perron fifty years later. The circulating claim of two independent recollections is wrong, and the variant 'OK, she'll do' appears in no fetched source. Month and day unknown.
stops.campa: A dancer in a Barbara Gardner piece is injured. Rudner learns the part and steps in, at Judson Hall on West Fifty-seventh Street beside Carnegie Hall. Margaret Jenkins brings Twyla Tharp to watch. Tharp stays a few minutes and leaves. What she says on the way out is two words, and it is the entire audition: a twenty-year working relationship begins with a stranger's glance at a substitution. The words reach Rudner through Jenkins, and reach anyone else when Rudner repeats them fifty years later. Nobody wrote them down at the time.
stops.quote: Margy said that Twyla came in [to see me dance] and stayed for a few minutes and said, "She'll do."
stops.quote_source: Sara Rudner, in Wendy Perron, 'Sara Rudner on Early Tharp' (1 December 2015)
suggested_refs: Judson Hall, 165 West 57th Street, since demolished
sources: Wendy Perron, 'Sara Rudner on Early Tharp' (2015)

stops.name: Broome Street, the loft economy
stops.date_confidence: attested for the street: Perron's interview names Broome Street as the neighborhood Rudner shared with Margaret Jenkins and, through her, Tharp. The month is a placeholder for the mid-1960s.
stops.campa: She lives on Broome Street, in the same few blocks as Margaret Jenkins and, through Jenkins, Tharp. The lofts are cheap because nobody wants them: cast-iron buildings zoned for light manufacturing, rented by dancers and painters who can tolerate no heat. The economics are the precondition for the work. An experimental dance that pays nothing is only possible where rent is nearly nothing. The downtown of the middle sixties is the last stretch in Manhattan when that is true.
sources: Wendy Perron, 'Sara Rudner on Early Tharp' (2015)

segments.name: Twyla Tharp and Dancers: The Task Years

stops.name: Judson Memorial Church, Re-Moves and the stopwatch
stops.date_confidence: attested by the Twyla Tharp Foundation's own work page, which gives the premiere as 29 October 1966 with the original cast, lighting, design and duration. A Wikipedia chronology of Tharp gives 18 October 1966 instead; the contradiction is recorded and not resolved, and the Foundation date is used. The rope ladder and the relevé zigzag appear in neither source.
stops.campa: Twyla Tharp, Sara Rudner and Margaret Jenkins perform Re-Moves at Judson Memorial Church on Washington Square, the audience seated on three sides with a curtain closing the fourth. Jennifer Tipton lights it, Robert Huot designs it, and it runs about forty-five minutes. The task is the choreography. The dancers measure the room heel to toe and work behind obstructions, and what the audience watches is labor rather than display. At the end the three of them disappear inside a box.
stops.quote: The first thing I ever did with Twyla was with a stopwatch; it was at Judson Church.
stops.quote_source: Sara Rudner, in Wendy Perron, 'Sara Rudner on Early Tharp' (1 December 2015)
suggested_refs: twylatharp.org/works/re-moves, the Foundation's own record of cast, design and duration
sources: Twyla Tharp Foundation, 'Re-Moves'
Wendy Perron, 'Sara Rudner on Early Tharp' (2015)

stops.name: Brooklyn Academy of Music, the desk and the dressing room
stops.date_confidence: attested by Perron's interview, which confirms the clerical job for the Merce Cunningham Dance Foundation in its BAM office. The year is a placeholder inside the mid-to-late 1960s; no source dates the employment precisely.
stops.campa: She takes clerical work in the Merce Cunningham Dance Foundation's office at the Brooklyn Academy of Music: typing, answering the phone, the ordinary administration of another choreographer's company. Between calls she goes into a dressing room and does barre, then returns to the desk. Merce Cunningham's foundation, incorporated a few years earlier, is paying her wage while Tharp's company pays nothing. This is how the downtown avant-garde is financed. No source dates the job, and she mentions it in passing, decades afterward.
sources: Wendy Perron, 'Sara Rudner on Early Tharp' (2015)

stops.name: Germany, the cut foot on a bad floor
stops.date_confidence: attested that the tour happened in 1967 and that Rudner names Germany for this incident in Perron's interview. Contradiction flagged: dossier material names the Netherlands, Paris and London for the same tour. Neither account gives a city, so the pin is a country centroid and the month is a placeholder.
stops.campa: The company tours Europe for the first time, a handful of dancers and no money. The work being carried across the Atlantic is task-based and unmusical, difficult to explain to a European presenter who has booked what he takes to be American modern dance. Rudner remembers Germany: a bad floor, and Tharp cutting her foot open on it and finishing the performance rather than stopping it. Nobody states the standard as a rule. It is demonstrated once, in front of everyone, and afterwards assumed.
stops.quote: As hard as we thought we worked, she worked twice as hard.
stops.quote_source: Sara Rudner, in Wendy Perron, 'Sara Rudner on Early Tharp' (1 December 2015)
sources: Wendy Perron, 'Sara Rudner on Early Tharp' (2015)

stops.name: Amherst, Sowing of Seeds across a field
stops.date_confidence: attested; the Twyla Tharp Foundation gives the premiere as 7 June 1970 at the University of Massachusetts-Amherst, on a field outside the Agricultural Department, and names the full cast, every member of which matches the dossier.
stops.campa: On a field outside the Agricultural Department at the University of Massachusetts, Douglas Dunn, Isabel Garcia-Lorca, Sara Rudner, Twyla Tharp and Rose Marie Wright form a long diagonal line with a group of students and scatter seeds out of tin cans. There is no stage, no lighting, and no frame except the field. The piece is called Sowing of Seeds and it does what it is called. The gesture is agricultural before it is choreographic, and at a distance the line is indistinguishable from a work crew. The date is the seventh of June, 1970.
sources: Twyla Tharp Foundation, 'Sowing of Seeds'

stops.name: Amherst, The Fugue on an amplified floor
stops.date_confidence: attested; the Twyla Tharp Foundation gives the premiere as 1 August 1970 at the University of Massachusetts-Amherst, cast Tharp, Rudner and Rose Marie Wright. Note that gathered chronologies collapsed this work and Re-Moves into a single 1970 entry; they are six years and two venues apart.
stops.campa: Two months later, on the same campus, Tharp, Rudner and Rose Marie Wright premiere The Fugue: twenty variations on a twenty-count phrase, danced in silence on an amplified floor, in boots. The sound the audience hears is the dancing itself, three women stamping out a structure borrowed from Bach. It is counted rather than felt, and learned by successive generations of dancers as a discipline. The Foundation calls it the first Tharp work intended to survive as active repertory rather than as an occasion.
sources: Twyla Tharp Foundation, 'The Fugue'

segments.name: The City as Stage, and the Long Form

stops.name: Fort Tryon Park, the dance begins at five in the morning
stops.date_confidence: attested; the Twyla Tharp Foundation gives 28 March 1971, three New York sites, Tharp, Rudner and Rose Marie Wright throughout, a 5 a.m. start, and the note that the work was performed only once in its entirety. The Foundation page glosses the park as Harlem; it is in Washington Heights.
stops.campa: At five in the morning, in Fort Tryon Park high above the Hudson, Tharp, Rudner and Rose Marie Wright begin Sunrise/Noon/Sundown. The park is empty at that hour and the light comes up during the dancing. The piece is built to occupy a whole day and a whole city rather than a stage and an evening: three sites, three times, one continuous work carried between them by the dancers themselves. It will be performed complete exactly once, and no film of the morning leg is known.
sources: Twyla Tharp Foundation, 'Sunrise/Noon/Sundown'

stops.name: Battery Park, the middle leg at midday
stops.date_confidence: attested as the midday site of Sunrise/Noon/Sundown by the Twyla Tharp Foundation. No account of what was danced there specifically survives in any fetched source.
stops.campa: By midday the three dancers are at the southern tip of Manhattan, in Battery Park, with the harbor behind them and a lunchtime crowd that has not come to see anything. The audience is whoever is present. The piece has been running seven hours, most of them spent travelling between the park at the top of the island and the park at the bottom, and the travelling is not an interruption of it. No account survives of what was danced here specifically. It is the middle of a work that will not finish until dark.
sources: Twyla Tharp Foundation, 'Sunrise/Noon/Sundown'

stops.name: City Hall, the day closes where the city administers itself
stops.date_confidence: attested as the evening site of Sunrise/Noon/Sundown by the Twyla Tharp Foundation.
stops.campa: The last leg is danced at City Hall in the evening, at the seat of the government of the city the piece has spent the day crossing. Dawn in Washington Heights, noon at the harbor, and now dusk at the municipal building. There is no ticket and no house. The three of them finish and go home. It is the twenty-eighth of March, 1971, and Sunrise/Noon/Sundown will never be given entire again. What the Foundation keeps of it afterwards is a cast list and a start time.
sources: Twyla Tharp Foundation, 'Sunrise/Noon/Sundown'

stops.name: Delacorte Theater, Eight Jelly Rolls
stops.date_confidence: attested; the Twyla Tharp Foundation gives the premiere date, the Delacorte, and the full original cast. Two dossier claims are dropped as unsupported: that this was Tharp's first proscenium work, and that the solos 'Mournful Serenade' and 'Shreveport Stomp' were Rudner's.
stops.campa: Eight Jelly Rolls premieres at the open-air Delacorte Theater in Central Park: Naomi Cohn, Mary Curry, Isabel Garcia-Lorca, Sara Rudner, Twyla Tharp and Rose Marie Wright, dancing to Jelly Roll Morton. After six years of stopwatches, bare fields and silence, the company plays jazz to an audience that laughs. This becomes the work people remember. The Foundation is still licensing it to ballet companies, universities and conservatories forty years later, danced by people who were not born when it was made.
suggested_refs: The Foundation's licensing record for Eight Jelly Rolls: Company C Ballet 2005, Barnard College 2007, Ethical Culture Fieldston School and George Mason 2008, Duke 2009, American Repertory Ballet, University of South Carolina and Yale 2011, Boston Conservatory 2012
sources: Twyla Tharp Foundation, 'Eight Jelly Rolls'

stops.name: St. Mark's Church in-the-Bowery, five hours of Dancing-on-View
stops.date_confidence: partly attested: Perron confirms the St. Mark's marathon dances beginning in 1975, and Wikipedia supplies the church address. The exact date of 10 June, the full cast, the Kushner backdrop and the red linoleum are reconstruction from dossier material.
stops.campa: In the sanctuary of St. Mark's Church in-the-Bowery, red linoleum and pews and cross still in place, Rudner makes Dancing-on-View and dances it for five hours with Wendy Perron, Wendy Rogers and Risa Jaroslow, against a pomegranate backdrop by Robert Kushner. The audience comes and goes. Five hours is not an endurance stunt but a condition: the dancers get tired, the dancing changes because they are tired, and the change is the material. This is her own work now, under her own name.
suggested_refs: The Wendy Perron Papers, 1973-2001, Fales Library and Special Collections, NYU (MSS.123), whose finding aid names Rudner among the choreographers Perron danced for
sources: Wendy Perron, wendyperron.com, on the St. Mark's marathon dances

stops.name: Goddard College, a barn solo called Yes
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the residency, the solo, its title and Meredith Monk's presence developing Quarry are dossier leads unsupported by any fetched source. Month is a placeholder for a summer residency. Coordinates corrected to the Pitkin Road campus, about 2 km southwest of the gathered figure.
stops.campa: At a summer residency at Goddard College in Vermont, in a barn, Rudner makes a semi-improvised solo she calls Yes. Meredith Monk is on the same campus developing Quarry. The title is the whole instruction: take what the body offers rather than editing it into something else first. Nothing of the solo is notated and nothing is filmed, and no fetched source confirms even that much. Who was standing in the barn, and whether anyone was, the record does not say.
sources: Dossier lead only; unconfirmed

stops.name: 541 Broadway, thirty-two dances for thirty-two years
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; dossier lead only, though internally consistent, since 16 February 1976 as a thirty-second birthday matches the confirmed 1944 birth exactly. Coordinates corrected roughly 400 m northeast to the actual Broadway address.
stops.campa: In Lucinda Childs's loft at 541 Broadway, on her thirty-second birthday, Rudner performs Some Yes and More: thirty-two discrete dances, one for each year. Siobhan Davies and Richard Alston, visiting from London, work the door as ushers. The loft is a working studio, not a theater, and the dances are made to fit it. The arithmetic is the form, and a birthday counted out in dances rather than candles turns a private date into a public structure. The audience sits on the floor. The count runs to thirty-two.
sources: Dossier lead only; unconfirmed

stops.name: Roundabout Theatre, the additive duets
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; dossier lead only for the venue and the duets. The Sara Rudner Performance Ensemble's 1976-1982 span comes from the Sarah Lawrence College retirement announcement of 19 June 2019, which returned HTTP 404 in this pass. Year is a placeholder inside the late 1970s.
stops.campa: With Wendy Rogers she makes additive duets at the Roundabout Theatre on West Twenty-sixth Street: material accumulates, one phrase set beside another and then both again with a third, so the dance grows by integration rather than by contrast. The Sara Rudner Performance Ensemble is running now, six years of it in the end. She is choreographer, director and dancer at once, and in this economy that also means booking the theater herself. The ensemble's dates rest on a single announcement page that no longer resolves.
sources: Dossier lead only; the ensemble's dates rest on the unretrievable Sarah Lawrence College announcement (19 June 2019)

segments.name: The Ensemble Closes, the Heart Opens

stops.name: SoHo, the retina and the fellowship
stops.date_confidence: the Guggenheim Fellowship in choreography is attested for 1981 by the Foundation's own fellows database. The detached retina is reconstruction, reported only as Rudner's own account, with no month, and the congenital amblyopia likewise. The pin is her attested SoHo neighborhood, used because no location is recorded for either event.
stops.campa: A retina detaches. The treatment is weeks flat on her back in a darkened room, which for a dancer is not convalescence but subtraction: the body that is the entire instrument stops being available. The same year the Guggenheim Foundation names her a fellow in choreography, an award arriving at the moment she cannot spend it. No month is recorded for the detachment. She has lived since birth with a fault in depth perception, one that kept her out of ball games and never once out of a studio.
suggested_refs: John Simon Guggenheim Memorial Foundation fellows database, gf.org, entry for 1981 in choreography
sources: John Simon Guggenheim Memorial Foundation, gf.org
Dossier lead only for the retina and the amblyopia

stops.name: SoHo, the ensemble stops
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the 1982 disbanding rests solely on the Sarah Lawrence College announcement of 19 June 2019, which returned HTTP 404. Rudner's linking of the decision to her convalescence is her own account and unconfirmed. Peggy Gould's 1987 start is from the same unretrievable page.
stops.campa: The Sara Rudner Performance Ensemble stops. Six years of dancers, bookings, rehearsal space and payroll close down, and she later connects the decision to the months spent on her back. Companies in this economy do not fail dramatically; one person decides not to raise the money again. She keeps dancing. What ends is the apparatus around the dancing, and she does not build another one for herself. Peggy Gould will begin working with her five years later and stay for decades.
sources: Sarah Lawrence College retirement announcement (19 June 2019), cited in dossier material but unretrievable, HTTP 404

stops.name: Cambridge, the apparatus in Janney's studio
stops.date_confidence: attested; Rudner's own first-person section in Christopher Janney's 2025 retrospective places the first encounter in his MIT studio in Cambridge and dates the choice to 1983. Month and day are unknown; the telemetry hardware by Transkinetics, Inc. is confirmed by MIT News (13 May 1998).
stops.campa: In Christopher Janney's studio at MIT she is shown a device: sensors that read a live heartbeat by wireless telemetry and turn it into sound. Janney puts two possible projects in front of her. She chooses this one on instinct, and dates the whole subsequent shape of her dancing to that choice. The apparatus is bioengineering hardware built by a company called Transkinetics, borrowed out of medicine and pointed at a stage. What it measures is exertion, in beats per minute, continuously.
stops.quote: My intuitive preference for "HeartBeat" defined the direction my dancing would take. It was 1983.
stops.quote_source: Sara Rudner, 'HEARTBEAT MEMORIES,' in Christopher Janney, '40 Years Passing By In (A) HeartBeat' (14 July 2025)
sources: Christopher Janney, '40 Years Passing By In (A) HeartBeat' (2025), Rudner's own section
MIT News, 'ArtHeart' (13 May 1998)

stops.name: Boston, HeartBeat at the Institute of Contemporary Art
stops.date_confidence: attested; MIT News (13 May 1998) states the work was premiered by Sara Rudner at Boston's Institute of Contemporary Art in 1983. Month unknown. Authorship corrected: the piece and its score are Janney's, with Rudner as its first dancer. Coordinates are the ICA's 1975-2006 home at 955 Boylston Street, not the present waterfront building.
stops.campa: At the Institute of Contemporary Art on Boylston Street she premieres HeartBeat, Janney's piece, wired to her own chest. Her heart drives a percussive score, the score drives her dancing, and the dancing drives her heart faster. The loop is closed and audible, and an audience hears exertion directly instead of inferring it from a face. The same season she dances Fait Accompli, which becomes her last contribution to Twyla Tharp's work. She and Janney will perform HeartBeat together on and off until 1990.
stops.quote_source: Sara Rudner in conversation with Rashaun Mitchell, Small Press Traffic, The Back Room (20 May 2025)

stops.name: Salzburg, the Dancing Angel at the Felsenreitschule
stops.date_confidence: the production is attested: Wikipedia confirms Saint Francois d'Assise was staged at the 1992 Salzburg Festival in the Felsenreitschule, directed by Peter Sellars, Salonen conducting the Los Angeles Philharmonic. Rudner's Dancing Angel role, the 17-28 August dates and Dawn Upshaw in the 1992 cast are confirmed by no fetched source. Sarah Lawrence's general Salzburg credit is on the 404'd page.
stops.campa: Peter Sellars stages Messiaen's Saint Francois d'Assise at the Felsenreitschule, the riding school cut into the rock face of the Monchsberg, with Esa-Pekka Salonen conducting the Los Angeles Philharmonic. Rudner is remembered as the Dancing Angel, a body doubling the singing Angel, red and winged, moving where a voice cannot go. It is the largest apparatus she has ever worked inside, and her part in it is silent. No fetched source puts her in the cast. The production is confirmed; her presence in it is not.

stops.name: Lincoln Center, the oral history
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the interview date and subject matter are dossier leads and were not independently located. Coordinates are for the library building generally.
stops.campa: She sits for an oral-history interview at the New York Public Library for the Performing Arts: earliest memories, family, Brooklyn, Barnard, the company years. The date carried for it is the nineteenth of February, 1995, and no reachable catalogue confirms that. The library is doing to her what libraries do to dancers, which is to convert a body of work that leaves no object behind into a recording of somebody talking about it. She is fifty-one and still performing, and the file is opened anyway.

stops.name: The Public Theater, choreographing The Skriker
stops.date_confidence: the production is attested: Wikipedia confirms the American debut of Caryl Churchill's The Skriker at the Public Theater in 1996 under Mark Wing-Davey, and Wikipedia's Rudner article independently confirms she choreographed for the Public Theater. Her credit on this specific production is reconstruction; publictheater.org returned HTTP 403. Month unknown.
stops.campa: At the Public Theater on Lafayette Street, Caryl Churchill's The Skriker has its American debut under Mark Wing-Davey, and Rudner choreographs the fairies: a large ensemble of shape-shifting creatures who have to move like nothing human without turning into a ballet. Theater choreography is a different trade from making dances. The movement must serve a text and survive eight shows a week, and it will be executed by actors rather than by dancers. She takes the work, and she takes more of it after.
sources: Wikipedia, 'The Skriker'

stops.name: Houston, moving The Greeks at the Alley Theatre
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; dossier lead only. Neither the production nor Rudner's credit was independently located. Month unknown.
stops.campa: In Houston she stages movement for The Greeks at the Alley Theatre, a two-part production running nearly forty actors through more than a hundred and fifty costumes, the tragedies compressed into one evening's architecture. Choruses have to move as a single body and then break apart on cue. It is the largest crowd she has ever handled and not one of them is a dancer. Her name goes in the program under movement rather than choreography. Neither the production nor her credit could be located in any reachable record.
sources: Dossier lead only; unconfirmed

stops.name: Paris, the heart lent to another body
stops.date_confidence: partly attested: Janney's 2025 document records that around 1997 Rudner called to say Baryshnikov was interested in the piece, and MIT News (13 May 1998) states he premiered it in Paris and New York before the Boston performances. No fetched source names MC93 Bobigny or any other venue, so that claim is dropped and the corpus's canonical Paris coordinates are used. Month unknown; the Baryshnikov 'hypnotic' quotation is unlocated.
stops.campa: The heartbeat piece is rebuilt for another chest. Mikhail Baryshnikov asks after it, Janney adapts the apparatus, and Heartbeat: mb premieres in Paris. The solo Rudner originated in a Boston museum in 1983 now runs through the most famous dancer alive, in front of audiences who have never heard of Judson Church. The venue that later accounts name cannot be confirmed by anything reachable. What is certain is the transfer: a work built around one woman's cardiac rhythm becomes a vehicle for a man's.

stops.campa: Heartbeat: mb reaches Boston's Shubert Theatre for four nights in May, part of White Oak Dance Project's ten-city American tour. The American version adds a string quartet and ends on Barber's Adagio for Strings, the amplified heart giving way to written music at the close. Fifteen years after the premiere a few miles across the same city, the piece comes back to Boston as a touring commodity with a star inside it and a subscription audience in front of it. Rudner is not the one dancing.

stops.campa: She goes back to school in her fifties, at Bennington College in the Vermont hills, for a graduate degree in choreography, studying with Terry Creach, Dana Reitz and Susan Sgorbati. Thirty years into a career that made her a name in New York, she submits herself again to a curriculum and to other people's assignments. The degree is not a credential she needs in order to dance. It is the credential required to run a college program, and she takes it before anyone has offered her one.

stops.campa: She takes the Dance Program at Sarah Lawrence College in Bronxville. The chair before her was Viola Farber, a founding dancer of Merce Cunningham's company, who led the department for a decade and died in office the winter before. Rudner arrives into a room still holding that. The college is small and its dancers are not conservatory-tracked. What they get is a working choreographer with thirty-five years of finding out what a body can be asked to do, and every intention of asking them. She stays twenty years.

stops.name: Sarah Lawrence College, composition beside technique

stops.campa: The program she builds puts composition and improvisation beside technique as daily practice rather than as electives taken after the real training. A student makes work from the first year. The premise is the one her own life demonstrates: dancing and making are not two careers, and the separation between the person who executes and the person who invents is an administrative convenience. Rose Anne Thom, long on the same faculty, used to say that dance is a way of knowing. Rudner runs the department as though that were settled.
stops.quote: I remain devoted to Dance as a way of being and knowing.

stops.campa: This Dancing Life is produced for the Kilkenny Arts Festival in the Irish midlands, another long-form work about dancing made visible over time rather than compressed into an event. The festival programs it among concerts and readings. Her titles tend to be flat and literal, and this one is no exception. The method has not changed since the marathon at St. Mark's thirty-two years earlier: put dancers in a room for longer than a concert lasts, and let the audience watch what happens to them. No festival programme for it could be found.

stops.campa: Necessary Weather returns to the Baryshnikov Arts Center, seventeen years after Dana Reitz conceived and structured it with Rudner and the lighting designer Jennifer Tipton. There is no music. Light is the third performer rather than the setting: it arrives, moves, and leaves, and the two dancers answer it. Both women are in their sixties. Deborah Jowitt, watching, writes that the movements are not performed by them so much as born in them, and notes that the dancing involves no high kicks and no big jumps.
stops.quote: Movements settle on them, tickle them, emanate from them, are born in them.

The college announces it in the ordinary way and lists the awards: a Guggenheim, a Bessie, the Dance Magazine Award, support from the National Endowment for the Arts and the New York State Council on the Arts. stops.campa: She moves west, to the East Bay, near her son Eli and his wife. A regular studio practice assembles around her: Risa Jaroslow and Wendy Rogers, with whom she danced the five-hour marathon at St. Mark's in 1975, and younger Bay Area dancers who were not alive for it. Two hip replacements and a revision are behind her. The practice is not a company, has no season, and produces nothing anyone can license. It is a standing appointment to keep dancing.

stops.date_confidence: the conversation is attested and dated 20 May 2025 by Small Press Traffic, which published it. stops.campa: In conversation with the choreographer Rashaun Mitchell, published in the spring of her eighty-second year, she looks back at HeartBeat and at leaving Tharp twice. Mitchell danced HeartBeat himself in 2000, downtown; she watched it, and tells him what she saw, that his body grew inside it, that he started the dance as Rashaun and ended it as Rashaun. Her account of her own departures is unsentimental. Exhaustion the first time, she says, and curiosity.
stops.quote: I learned how to work from Twyla Tharp.
stops.quote_source: Sara Rudner in conversation with Rashaun Mitchell, Small Press Traffic, The Back Room (20 May 2025)
